execute: freeze: true is set globally in _quarto.yml. This means:

R code chunks are only executed once. Results are cached in _freeze/.
On subsequent renders Quarto uses the cached output — it does not re-run R.
This keeps the build fast and reproducible without needing R dependencies installed on the server.

Exceptions: The Projects, Speaking, Software, Publications, and CV (cv/cv-page.qmd) pages all have freeze: false set in their YAML header, so they always re-execute when rendered. The Publications page also sets flush = TRUE in get_publications() to bypass the scholar package cache and requests the complete profile list. Projects, Speaking, Software, and CV can be rendered directly after changing their data sources; Publications refreshes from Google Scholar on every render.

The hero background canvas has an interactive feature on top of the particle animation:

A hint (“Click anywhere to place data points”) appears in the top-right in site-blue (#007BFF) at opacity 0.65, fading very slowly (hidden when viewport width < 700px so it doesn’t collide with the heading on mobile).
Clicking on the background (not on links/buttons) places a blue dot with a white border and a pop-in animation. A counter (“3 / 10”) tracks progress.
At 10 dots, a LOESS curve (span = 0.75, tricube kernel) is fitted through the points and drawn as a solid blue line. The R² value and the message “This is basically my job :)” appear in the top-right corner of the canvas.
A “⟳ Random data” button appears just below the tagline (top-right, top: 56px; hidden below 700px on mobile). Clicking it clears any existing dots, generates 10 new random points spread across the canvas, and immediately fits + displays the LOESS and R². Clicking it again regenerates a fresh random set.
Clicking anywhere on the canvas (11th click, or first click after a random set) clears everything and the cycle restarts.




Quarto 1.9+ can hoist the first hero heading into the page title block when it sees an <h1> inside the landing-page HTML. The hero now uses .hero_title instead, and #title-block-header is hidden in html/landing_page_styles.css so the landing page stays flush under the navbar.
The hero uses 6rem of top padding and aligns .hero_content to the start so the “Hi, I’m Lasai” heading remains below the pinned navbar instead of being vertically centered on desktop.
Key parameters in the <script> block of index.qmd: - MAX_DOTS — number of points before the curve is drawn (default: 10) - 0.75 in computeLoess() — the LOESS span (smoothing parameter) - hintOpacity — initial opacity of the hint text (default: 0.65) - top: 56px in #random-btn CSS — positions the button below the “This is basically my job :)” line
Resizing the browser window clears dots and resets the hint.

The page appears as “Talks” in the navbar (renamed from “Speaking”). The page has two sections:

Timeline — a filter pill bar (All | Talks | Posters, .tl-filter-bar / .tl-filter-btn in html/timeline.css) lets visitors filter by presentation type (data-type / data-year), and an R chunk (tl-speaking) reads the Excel, builds HTML cards, and outputs them via cat() with results='asis'. Shares timeline CSS with the projects page via html/timeline.css. Year dividers are automatically inserted between entries from different years (and hidden automatically when no entries in that year match the active filter).
Map — an R chunk (map-data) reads conferences.xlsx with openxlsx, checks a local geocoding cache (speaking/geocache.csv), queries ArcGIS only for new/uncached cities, and injects the coordinates as JSON for the Leaflet interactive map.

The map uses Leaflet.js with public OpenStreetMap tiles, so it does not require an API key. Conference locations and affiliated institutions are geocoded from their city names at render time using the ArcGIS geocoder and persisted in speaking/geocache.csv so subsequent renders are fast and work offline. Rendering stops with a clear error if the geocoding service is unavailable for an uncached city or returns no result, rather than generating a map without points. Clicking any marker opens a styled popup. The map works on both desktop and mobile with native touch support. Zoom is constrained (minZoom: 2, maxBounds) so only a single world view is shown.


Each timeline entry has a unique id attribute (e.g., talk-iscb-2024), generated in R from Code_Name and Year with make.unique(..., sep = "-") so multiple talks at the same conference/year stay distinct. Both tl-speaking and map-data sort by -Year, -Month so IDs match identically.

Map → timeline: Conference markers are grouped by city so multiple talks in the same city share one marker instead of stacking; its popup lists every talk at that city, each with its own “Show in timeline ↓” link (window._scrollToEntry). Clicking it resets any active filter if needed, smooth-scrolls to the matching timeline entry, and applies a 2-second blue pulse highlight (tl-highlight class → tl-flash animation in html/timeline.css).
Timeline → map: Every timeline card includes a “Locate on map ↑” link (window._focusMapEntry) that smooth-scrolls to the map, pans/zooms to that city’s marker, and opens its popup.

The page pulls your publication list live from Google Scholar (user ID uPOL3NkAAAAJ) using the scholar R package (flush = TRUE), resolves complete author lists for truncated entries (...), filters out non-authored entries (such as award announcements about you), and builds the interactive D3 co-authorship network and searchable publication list.



Run quarto render Publications/publications-page.qmd (or render the full site).
The R code fetches the complete profile list (flush = TRUE), resolves full author lists, re-runs deduplication, and rebuilds both graphNodes/graphLinks and allPublications.




Google Scholar truncates multi-author entries in the profile table with , ... and scholar::get_complete_authors() frequently returns NA under Google Scholar rate limits. For every truncated paper, graph-data resolves full author lists through a 4-tier fallback chain (formatted cleanly to Initials Surname while preserving multi-word particles like Van Calster, van Smeden, De Cock Campo and corporate groups like IOTA 6 Collaborators):

Layer 1 — Local BibTeX files (cv/peer_bib_auto.bib, cv/other_bib_auto.bib, cv/peer_bib.bib, in priority order) matched by normalized title Jaccard similarity (>= 0.75). Handles Zotero trailing particles (e.g., Calster, Ben Van), BibLaTeX family=.../prefix=... entries, and braced group authors.
Layer 2a — OpenAlex ORCID works (https://api.openalex.org/works?filter=author.orcid:https://orcid.org/0000-0001-8020-0210&per-page=100) matched by normalized title Jaccard similarity (>= 0.70), excluding type == "dataset" and Replication Data / Correction / Erratum records.
Layer 2b — OpenAlex title search fallback (>= 0.75 similarity, verified to contain a Barreñada author), also excluding datasets/corrections.
Layer 3 — scholar::get_complete_authors() fallback if still unresolved.

After full author resolution, any Scholar entry where no author matches barre[nñ] (such as third-party prize announcements) is excluded. Malformed Scholar venue strings (e.g., arXiv preprint arXiv:, :2610.37353) are formatted cleanly (arXiv:2610.37353), and Clean_pubs / pubs_by_author / allPublications are consistently ordered by -year, -cites.



Two-stage canonicalization handles surface variants and initial differences:

manual_corrections near the middle of graph-data maps abbreviations, particles, and encoding artefacts before automated grouping:

manual_corrections <- c(
  "G Collins"        = "GS Collins",
  "JF Calatrava"     = "J Fernández Calatrava",
  "JCGS de Cueto"    = "JC Gálvez Sainz de Cueto",
  "JYJ Verbakel"     = "JY Verbakel",
  "BV Calster"       = "B Van Calster",
  "BD Moor"          = "B De Moor",
  "BDC Campo"        = "B De Cock Campo",
  "B De Cock"        = "B De Cock Campo",
  "TH Bourne"        = "T Bourne",
  "RR Zegarra"       = "R Ramirez Zegarra",
  "Rén Armañanzas"   = "R Armañanzas"
)

Stage 1 (accent/case preference) groups names sharing the same transliterated lowercase key (M Martinez-Garcia ≡ M Martínez-García), preferring forms with accented Unicode characters, longer initials, and higher frequency.
Stage 2 (initial-prefix merge with co-occurrence guard) automatically merges unambiguous initial prefixes sharing an exact surname (e.g., A Vickers → AJ Vickers, E Steyerberg → EW Steyerberg) only when the two forms have zero co-occurrence on the same paper — preventing distinct authors like H Lee and HC Lee on the Nature Medicine paper from being merged. Corporate/consortium names (Collaborators, Consortium, Group, Committee) are kept in the paper’s authors string but excluded from collaborator counts.

If a new co-author appears under an unexpected abbreviation or nickname, add an entry to manual_corrections:
"Garbled form"  = "Canonical form"



The pipeline detects preprint/working-paper duplicates (arxiv|biorxiv|medrxiv|zenodo|preprint|working paper|statistics spain) by comparing titles with Jaccard similarity. If a preprint on Google Scholar gets published and both entries appear simultaneously, the preprint is dropped when Jaccard similarity ≥ 0.28 with a published paper.



This is controlled by the filter(n_papers >= 2) line in the R chunk. Change 2 to any other threshold if needed. Co-authors are ordered via hierarchical clustering (stats::hclust(..., method = "average") on a binary co-author × paper matrix) and assigned order_idx so D3 initializes research communities in adjacent radial sectors.



The network (W = 860, H = 600) uses several visual and usability enhancements in the <script> block:

Scaled radial geometry & clustered initialization: colorScale, rScale ([8, 22]), and distScale ([225, 92]) scale over actual [minP, maxP] counts so outer nodes stay cleanly inside the SVG bounds (padX = 56, padTop = 30, padBottom = 28), initialized by order_idx with light centering forces and collision radius + 22.
Focus + dim: Hovering or clicking a node highlights it and its connected links/nodes; everything else fades to 12% opacity (DIM_OPACITY). When a node is selected (clicked), hover on other nodes does not change the focus — only clicking a new node or the background changes it.
Label halos & clamped tooltips: Co-author surname labels render with a #f4f8fd paint-order: stroke halo for legibility across links, and #graph-tooltip coordinates are clamped inside #graph-container bounds. The legend dynamically renders actual minP and maxP shared-paper counts.
Mobile touch hit targets: Transparent overlay circles (hitSel, minimum radius 20 px) handle pointer, drag, and tap events so smaller co-author nodes remain easy to tap on touch screens.
Gradient nodes & curved links: Each node uses a radial gradient + drop shadow (center node uses center-glow); links alternate quadratic Bézier curve direction (sign = i % 2).
Full searchable publication list (#pub-list-section): Below the chart, R injects allPublications (deduplicated, sorted by -year, -cites) and JS renders a publication list with a live search box (#pub-search), a Sort: Year | Citations toggle (.pub-sort-btn — Year groups entries under year headers; Citations renders a flat list sorted by citation count with year badges), author self-highlighting, preprint/citation badges, and a count indicator. Clicking any co-author node in the D3 network filters #pub-full-list directly and highlights the selected collaborator’s links (clicking the node again, clicking the center node, clicking the SVG background, or clicking the filter pill’s × clears the filter and restores all publications).

Build-time cache (github-build-cache): At render time, R fetches owned repos and CONTRIB_REPOS from GitHub’s API (using curl with a User-Agent header when available) and embeds trimmed metadata in window.GITHUB_BUILD_CACHE.
Instant render + live refresh: On page load, if window.GITHUB_BUILD_CACHE is populated, cards render immediately with zero spinner flash. A background fetch() to https://api.github.com/users/LasaiBarrenada/repos?type=owner&sort=pushed&per_page=100 (plus CONTRIB_REPOS) refreshes star counts and push dates. If the live request fails (e.g., 403 unauthenticated rate limit on shared institutional Wi-Fi), the build-time cards remain visible instead of showing an error.
Repos are displayed in a responsive 2-column card grid (1 column on mobile), sorted by stars descending. Each card shows the repo name (linked), description, primary language with a coloured dot, star count, contributor badge (if applicable), topic tags, and a relative “Updated X ago” timestamp.

The gitlab-projects R chunk queries both https://gitlab.kuleuven.be/api/v4/users/u0158158/projects?per_page=100 and .../contributed_projects?per_page=100 at build time, deduplicates by project id, excludes archived projects and gitlab_exclude (u0158158), sorts by last_activity_at descending, and fetches /api/v4/projects/{id}/languages for each project (preferring programming languages such as R over HTML/CSS/SCSS/JavaScript). Cards display the full path_with_namespace, a red-orange "GitLab" badge (.sw-gitlab-badge), description, topic pills (.sw-topic-gitlab), primary language dot, and "Updated Mon YYYY".



The OSF API does not support CORS, so OSF data is fetched at build time by an R chunk (osf-projects), not in the browser. The R code calls https://api.osf.io/v2/users/pgkjv/nodes/ using jsonlite::fromJSON(), filters to top-level public projects (where root.data.id == node.id), and generates HTML cards via cat() with results='asis'. The page has freeze: false so OSF data refreshes on every render.
Cards show the project title (linked to OSF), an “OSF” badge (dark blue #214370), category label, description, tags, related paper links (if any), child components (if any), and an absolute date (“Updated Mar 2026”). Cards are sorted by most recently modified.



Each OSF card fetches its first-level child components via /nodes/{id}/children/ at render time (one API call per top-level project). Children are shown in a shaded box labelled “Components” with a left navy border. Each child is a linked item showing an emoji icon (by category), the component title, and a small category label. All child categories are shown.

The GitHub public API allows 60 requests/hour without authentication. Because github-build-cache embeds build-time data in window.GITHUB_BUILD_CACHE, visitors on shared networks won’t hit a broken empty page if the live browser fetch is rate-limited (the error fallback only appears if both the live fetch and build-time cache are unavailable).
The OSF public API has no documented unauthenticated rate limit, but is similarly generous. If it fails, a fallback message with a link to the OSF profile is shown.
Archived repos are automatically excluded (GitHub). Forked repos are filtered out from the main fetch.
To showcase external repos the user contributes to (via commits/PRs), add the upstream owner/repo path to the CONTRIB_REPOS array — these are fetched individually and shown with a “Contributor” badge.
Each entry in CONTRIB_REPOS uses one extra API call, so keep the list short to stay within the 60 req/hr limit.

execute: freeze: true is set globally in _quarto.yml. This means:

R code chunks are only executed once. Results are cached in _freeze/.
On subsequent renders Quarto uses the cached output — it does not re-run R.
This keeps the build fast and reproducible without needing R dependencies installed on the server.

Exceptions: The Projects, Speaking, Software, Publications, and CV (cv/cv-page.qmd) pages all have freeze: false set in their YAML header, so they always re-execute when rendered. The Publications page also sets flush = TRUE in get_publications() to bypass the scholar package cache and requests the complete profile list. Projects, Speaking, Software, and CV can be rendered directly after changing their data sources; Publications refreshes from Google Scholar on every render.

A hint (“Click anywhere to place data points”) appears in the top-right in site-blue (#007BFF) at opacity 0.65, fading very slowly (hidden when viewport width < 700px so it doesn’t collide with the heading on mobile).

A “⟳ Random data” button appears just below the tagline (top-right, top: 56px; hidden below 700px on mobile). Resizing the browser window clears dots and resets the hint.

Map — an R chunk (map-data) reads conferences.xlsx with openxlsx, checks a local geocoding cache (speaking/geocache.csv), queries ArcGIS only for new/uncached cities, and injects the coordinates as JSON for the Leaflet interactive map.

The map uses Leaflet.js with public OpenStreetMap tiles, so it does not require an API key. Conference locations and affiliated institutions are geocoded from their city names at render time using the ArcGIS geocoder and persisted in speaking/geocache.csv so subsequent renders are fast and work offline. Rendering stops with a clear error if the geocoding service is unavailable for an uncached city or returns no result, rather than generating a map without points. Clicking any marker opens a styled popup. The map works on both desktop and mobile with native touch support. Zoom is constrained (minZoom: 2, maxBounds) so only a single world view is shown.


Each timeline entry has a unique id attribute (e.g., talk-iscb-2024), generated in R from Code_Name and Year with make.unique(..., sep = "-") so multiple talks at the same conference/year stay distinct. Both tl-speaking and map-data sort by -Year, -Month so IDs match identically.

Map → timeline: Conference markers are grouped by city so multiple talks in the same city share one marker instead of stacking; its popup lists every talk at that city, each with its own “Show in timeline ↓” link (window._scrollToEntry). text:
The page pulls your publication list live from Google Scholar (user ID uPOL3NkAAAAJ) using the scholar R package (flush = TRUE), resolves complete author lists for truncated entries (...), filters out non-authored entries (such as award announcements about you), and builds the interactive D3 co-authorship network and searchable publication list.



Run quarto render Publications/publications-page.qmd (or render the full site).
The R code fetches the complete profile list (flush = TRUE), resolves full author lists, re-runs deduplication, and rebuilds both graphNodes/graphLinks and allPublications.




Google Scholar truncates multi-author entries in the profile table with , ... and scholar::get_complete_authors() frequently returns NA under Google Scholar rate limits. For every truncated paper, graph-data resolves full author lists through a 4-tier fallback chain (formatted cleanly to Initials Surname while preserving multi-word particles like Van Calster, van Smeden, De Cock Campo and corporate groups like IOTA 6 Collaborators):

Layer 1 — Local BibTeX files (cv/peer_bib_auto.bib, cv/other_bib_auto.bib, cv/peer_bib.bib, in priority order) matched by normalized title Jaccard similarity (>= 0.75). Handles Zotero trailing particles (e.g., Calster, Ben Van), BibLaTeX family=.../prefix=... entries, and braced group authors.
Layer 2a — OpenAlex ORCID works (https://api.openalex.org/works?filter=author.orcid:https://orcid.org/0000-0001-8020-0210&per-page=100) matched by normalized title Jaccard similarity (>= 0.70), excluding type == "dataset" and Replication Data / Correction / Erratum records.
Layer 2b — OpenAlex title search fallback (>= 0.75 similarity, verified to contain a Barreñada author), also excluding datasets/corrections.
Layer 3 — scholar::get_complete_authors() fallback if still unresolved.

After full author resolution, any Scholar entry where no author matches barre[nñ] (such as third-party prize announcements) is excluded. Malformed Scholar venue strings (e.g., arXiv preprint arXiv:, :2610.37353) are formatted cleanly (arXiv:2610.37353), and Clean_pubs / pubs_by_author / allPublications are consistently ordered by -year, -cites.



Two-stage canonicalization handles surface variants and initial differences:

manual_corrections near the middle of graph-data maps abbreviations, particles, and encoding artefacts before automated grouping:

manual_corrections <- c(
  "G Collins"        = "GS Collins",
  "JF Calatrava"     = "J Fernández Calatrava",
  "JCGS de Cueto"    = "JC Gálvez Sainz de Cueto",
  "JYJ Verbakel"     = "JY Verbakel",
  "BV Calster"       = "B Van Calster",
  "BD Moor"          = "B De Moor",
  "BDC Campo"        = "B De Cock Campo",
  "B De Cock"        = "B De Cock Campo",
  "TH Bourne"        = "T Bourne",
  "RR Zegarra"       = "R Ramirez Zegarra",
  "Rén Armañanzas"   = "R Armañanzas"
)

Stage 1 (accent/case preference) groups names sharing the same transliterated lowercase key (M Martinez-Garcia ≡ M Martínez-García), preferring forms with accented Unicode characters, longer initials, and higher frequency.
Stage 2 (initial-prefix merge with co-occurrence guard) automatically merges unambiguous initial prefixes sharing an exact surname (e.g., A Vickers → AJ Vickers, E Steyerberg → EW Steyerberg) only when the two forms have zero co-occurrence on the same paper — preventing distinct authors like H Lee and HC Lee on the Nature Medicine paper from being merged. Corporate/consortium names (Collaborators, Consortium, Group, Committee) are kept in the paper’s authors string but excluded from collaborator counts.

If a new co-author appears under an unexpected abbreviation or nickname, add an entry to manual_corrections:
"Garbled form"  = "Canonical form"



The pipeline detects preprint/working-paper duplicates (arxiv|biorxiv|medrxiv|zenodo|preprint|working paper|statistics spain) by comparing titles with Jaccard similarity. If a preprint on Google Scholar gets published and both entries appear simultaneously, the preprint is dropped when Jaccard similarity ≥ 0.28 with a published paper.



This is controlled by the filter(n_papers >= 2) line in the R chunk. Change 2 to any other threshold if needed. Co-authors are ordered via hierarchical clustering (stats::hclust(..., method = "average") on a binary co-author × paper matrix) and assigned order_idx so D3 initializes research communities in adjacent radial sectors.



The network (W = 860, H = 600) uses several visual and usability enhancements in the <script> block:

Scaled radial geometry & clustered initialization: colorScale, rScale ([8, 22]), and distScale ([225, 92]) scale over actual [minP, maxP] counts so outer nodes stay cleanly inside the SVG bounds (padX = 56, padTop = 30, padBottom = 28), initialized by order_idx with light centering forces and collision radius + 22.
Focus + dim: Hovering or clicking a node highlights it and its connected links/nodes; everything else fades to 12% opacity (DIM_OPACITY). When a node is selected (clicked), hover on other nodes does not change the focus — only clicking a new node or the background changes it.
Label halos & clamped tooltips: Co-author surname labels render with a #f4f8fd paint-order: stroke halo for legibility across links, and #graph-tooltip coordinates are clamped inside #graph-container bounds. The legend dynamically renders actual minP and maxP shared-paper counts.
Mobile touch hit targets: Transparent overlay circles (hitSel, minimum radius 20 px) handle pointer, drag, and tap events so smaller co-author nodes remain easy to tap on touch screens.
Gradient nodes & curved links: Each node uses a radial gradient + drop shadow (center node uses center-glow); links alternate quadratic Bézier curve direction (sign = i % 2).
Full searchable publication list (#pub-list-section): Below the chart, R injects allPublications (deduplicated, sorted by -year, -cites) and JS renders a publication list with a live search box (#pub-search), a Sort: Year | Citations toggle (.pub-sort-btn — Year groups entries under year headers; Citations renders a flat list sorted by citation count with year badges), author self-highlighting, preprint/citation badges, and a count indicator. Clicking any co-author node in the D3 network filters #pub-full-list directly and highlights the selected collaborator’s links (clicking the node again, clicking the center node, clicking the SVG background, or clicking the filter pill’s × clears the filter and restores all publications).

text:
The page displays repositories from three platforms (freeze: false):

GitHub (username LasaiBarrenada) — pre-fetched at build time by R (github-build-cache chunk) into window.GITHUB_BUILD_CACHE for instant rendering, and refreshed in the browser via client-side JS.
GitLab (KU Leuven) (username u0158158 at gitlab.kuleuven.be) — owned and contributed public projects fetched at build time by R (gitlab-projects chunk) and displayed under GitLab Projects (KU Leuven).
OSF (user ID pgkjv) — public top-level projects fetched at build time by R (osf-projects chunk) and displayed in a separate card grid below.




Build-time cache (github-build-cache): At render time, R fetches owned repos and CONTRIB_REPOS from GitHub’s API (using curl with a User-Agent header when available) and embeds trimmed metadata in window.GITHUB_BUILD_CACHE.
Instant render + live refresh: On page load, if window.GITHUB_BUILD_CACHE is populated, cards render immediately with zero spinner flash. A background fetch() to https://api.github.com/users/LasaiBarrenada/repos?type=owner&sort=pushed&per_page=100 (plus CONTRIB_REPOS) refreshes star counts and push dates. If the live request fails (e.g., 403 unauthenticated rate limit on shared institutional Wi-Fi), the build-time cards remain visible instead of showing an error.
Repos are displayed in a responsive 2-column card grid (1 column on mobile), sorted by stars descending. Each card shows the repo name (linked), description, primary language with a coloured dot, star count, contributor badge (if applicable), topic tags, and a relative “Updated X ago” timestamp.











Variable
Purpose




USERNAME
GitHub username to fetch repos from (currently LasaiBarrenada)


EXCLUDE_REPOS
Array of repo names to hide — currently LasaiBarrenada.github.io (website), LasaiBarrenada (profile config), web_resources (web assets)


CONTRIB_REPOS
Array of owner/repo strings for external repos the user contributes to — fetched individually and shown with a “Contributor” badge


LANG_COLORS
Map of language names → hex colours for the dot indicator






The gitlab-projects R chunk queries both https://gitlab.kuleuven.be/api/v4/users/u0158158/projects?per_page=100 and .../contributed_projects?per_page=100 at build time, deduplicates by project id, excludes archived projects and gitlab_exclude (u0158158), sorts by last_activity_at descending, and fetches /api/v4/projects/{id}/languages for each project (preferring programming languages such as R over HTML/CSS/SCSS/JavaScript). Cards display the full path_with_namespace, a red-orange "GitLab" badge (.sw-gitlab-badge), description, topic pills (.sw-topic-gitlab), primary language dot, and "Updated Mon YYYY".



The OSF API does not support CORS, so OSF data is fetched at build time by an R chunk (osf-projects), not in the browser. The R code calls https://api.osf.io/v2/users/pgkjv/nodes/ using jsonlite::fromJSON(), filters to top-level public projects (where root.data.id == node.id), and generates HTML cards via cat() with results='asis'. The page has freeze: false so OSF data refreshes on every render.
Cards show the project title (linked to OSF), an “OSF” badge (dark blue #214370), category label, description, tags, related paper links (if any), child components (if any), and an absolute date (“Updated Mar 2026”). Cards are sorted by most recently modified.



Each OSF card fetches its first-level child components via /nodes/{id}/children/ at render time (one API call per top-level project). Children are shown in a shaded box labelled “Components” with a left navy border. Each child is a linked item showing an emoji icon (by category), the component title, and a small category label. All child categories are shown.



Each OSF card can show links to associated published papers. Papers are looked up from two sources (both are merged):

projects/projects.xlsx — if a row has a value in the OSF_ID column matching the OSF node ID, the paper title and Link_1 URL are shown on the card. This is the preferred method since it avoids duplicating paper metadata.
osf_extra_papers — a named list in the R chunk for papers that are not in projects.xlsx. Add entries like:

osf_extra_papers <- list(
  "uxvhq" = list(list(title = "Paper title", url = "https://doi.org/..."))
)
Multiple papers per project are supported in both sources.










Variable
Purpose




OSF user ID
Hardcoded in the API URL (pgkjv) — change there if needed


cat_labels
Named vector mapping OSF category slugs → friendly display labels


osf_extra_papers
Named list of extra paper links for OSF projects not in projects.xlsx


truncate_title()

The GitHub public API allows 60 requests/hour without authentication. Because github-build-cache embeds build-time data in window.GITHUB_BUILD_CACHE, visitors on shared networks won’t hit a broken empty page if the live browser fetch is rate-limited (the error fallback only appears if both the live fetch and build-time cache are unavailable).
The OSF public API has no documented unauthenticated rate limit, but is similarly generous. If it fails, a fallback message with a link to the OSF profile is shown.
Archived repos are automatically excluded (GitHub). Forked repos are filtered out from the main fetch.
To showcase external repos the user contributes to (via commits/PRs), add the upstream owner/repo path to the CONTRIB_REPOS array — these are fetched individually and shown with a “Contributor” badge.
Each entry in CONTRIB_REPOS uses one extra API call, so keep the list short to stay within the 60 req/hr limit.

          Hi, I'm Lasai.
            I'm a medical statistician dedicated to developing, validating, and improving clinical prediction models to aid medical decision-making focusing on honest and transparent development and evaluation of these models.
            
            
            I'm an FWO Postdoctoral fellow at KU Leuven in the Development and Regeneration department and within the International Ovarian Tumour Analysis (IOTA) group, working with  Ben Van Calster, Laure Wynants, and Dirk Timmerman. Methodology Accepted

Nov 2026


The Fundamental Problem of Individual Risk Prediction


Journal of Clinical Epidemiology


Clinical prediction models are evaluated at the population level, yet decisions are made for individuals. Using real and synthetic ovarian cancer data, we trained 59,400 model variants and show that individual risk estimates are far more uncertain than commonly assumed—model uncertainty and applicability uncertainty often dominate estimation uncertainty, even for models that perform well overall. We argue that predictive algorithms should inform rather than dictate clinical care.

Nov 2026


The Problem of Continuous Endpoints for Clinical Decision Making: A Decision Curve Analysis Approach


Diagnostic and Prognostic Research


Decision curve analysis (DCA) is widely used for binary outcomes, yet extending it to continuous endpoints implicitly assumes linear clinical utility. Using simulations and a pain-reduction case study, we show that while thresholded continuous DCA can rank models and detect miscalibration, converting continuous predictions into probabilities of crossing clinically meaningful thresholds provides clearer clinical decision support.


Read more ▸

ADNEX2: Updating the ADNEX Risk Model for Surgically and Conservatively Managed Patients


medRxiv · Submitted to BMJ


We updated the ADNEX ultrasound-based ovarian cancer prediction model using data from 6,847 surgically and conservatively managed patients across 17 European centres. Applied as a two-step strategy after benign descriptors, ADNEX2 achieved an AUC of 0.95 and substantially improved calibration (O:E ratio 1.05 vs. 1.14 for ADNEX) across both operated and follow-up populations.


Read more ▸

Cost-Based Variable Selection for Prediction Models (NBvarsel)


arXiv · Submitted to JAMIA


Conventional variable selection optimizes statistical fit while ignoring predictor costs, burden, or invasiveness. We propose a decision-analytic variable selection framework using cross-validated Net Benefit that retains predictors only when their clinical utility gain outweighs measurement harm, accompanied by the NBvarsel R package on CRAN.


Read more ▸

An interactive R Shiny web application to visualize and assess calibration of clinical prediction models, making flexible calibration diagnostics accessible to researchers and clinicians without coding.

Methodology Published

Dec 2025


Clustered Flexible Calibration Curves Using Random Effects


Research Synthesis Methods


Model calibration may vary across hospitals or datasets, yet existing tools rarely account for this clustering. We propose and compare three approaches—clustered group calibration, two-stage meta-analysis, and mixed-model calibration—validated in simulations and a multi-centre case study (N = 2,489 ovarian tumours). We recommend two-stage meta-analysis with splines for estimating the overall curve and prediction interval, and mixed-model calibration for cluster-specific curves.


Read more ▸


PaperCodePackage





Methodology Published

Dec 2025


Evaluation of Performance Measures for Predictive AI Models


The Lancet Digital Health


We evaluated 32 performance measures across five domains (discrimination, calibration, overall performance, classification, and clinical utility) for validating predictive AI models in medicine. We identify two key properties for selecting appropriate measures: whether the measure is proper and whether it captures statistical vs. decision-analytical performance. Classification measures—including the F1 score—performed poorly in most clinically relevant settings. We recommend AUC, calibration plots, and net benefit as essential reporting measures.


Read more ▸

ADNEX vs. RMI: Head-to-Head Systematic Review & Meta-Analysis


BMJ Open


We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 studies (8,271 tumours) directly comparing the ADNEX and RMI models for ovarian malignancy diagnosis. ADNEX (AUC 0.92) substantially outperformed RMI (AUC 0.85), and was clinically useful in 96% of operated patients compared to 15% for RMI at standard decision thresholds. Most included studies were at high risk of bias due to incomplete reporting and poor methodology.


Read more ▸

Sep 2024


Random Forests and Overfitting: Visualization & Simulation Study


Diagnostic and Prognostic Research


Random forests routinely produce near-perfect training c-statistics in clinical risk prediction, raising concerns about overfitting. Through heatmap visualizations and a simulation study across 192 scenarios, we show this arises from local probability spikes around training events—a structural feature of the algorithm. Despite this, test c-statistics remained competitive, though calibration was consistently poor, challenging the recommendation to use fully grown trees when the goal is probability estimation.

ADNEX Model: Systematic Review & Meta-Analysis of External Validations


BMJ Medicine


We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of 47 external validation studies (17,007 tumours) of the ADNEX model for ovarian cancer diagnosis across 43 centres in 18 countries. The summary AUC was 0.93 (95% PI 0.85–0.98) both with and without CA125, with a 95% estimated probability of clinical usefulness in a new centre. A key limitation was that 91% of validations had a high risk of bias, and model calibration was rarely assessed.
